(p-163) **Surat al-Shu'ara' (The Poets)**

It is entirely Meccan. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: except for four verses from it, which were revealed in Medina, from His saying ﴿And the poets, the erring follow them﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 224] to its end.

The first: it is one of the names of Allah, by which He swore, and the object of the oath is ﴿If We willed, We could send down upon them﴾. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it is one of the names of the Qur'an. This was said by Qatadah.

The third: it is among the openings with which Allah began His Book. This was said by al-Hasan.

(p-164) The fourth: they are disjointed letters (huruf hija' muqatta'ah, the separate letters of the alphabet used at the start of some surahs) drawn from the names and attributes of Allah. As for the Ta', there are two views:

The first: it is from al-Tul (the Most Bountiful).

The second: it is from al-Tahir (the Pure).

As for the Sin, there are three views:

The first: it is from al-Quddus (the Most Holy).

The second: it is from al-Sami' (the All-Hearing).

The third: it is from al-Salam (the Source of Peace).

As for the Mim, there are three views:

The first: it is from al-Majid (the Most Glorious).

The second: it is from al-Rahim (the Most Merciful).

The third: it is from al-Malik (the King).

For the people of spiritual insight (ashab al-khawatir), there are two views on the interpretation of this:

The first: the Ta' is the tree of Tuba, the Sin is the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary (sidrat al-muntaha), and the Mim is Muhammad the Chosen (ﷺ).

The second: the Ta' is the delight (tarab) of those who repent, the Sin is Allah's veiling (satr) of the sinners, and the Mim is His knowledge of those who go astray. (p-١٦٦) His words, ﴿and my chest tightens﴾: meaning, I fear that my heart will constrict. On this there are two views:

﴿So send to Harun﴾: meaning, so that he may be a messenger with me, because Harun was in Egypt, where God Most High had sent Musa as a prophet.

(p-169) His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿So he threw down his staff﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it was of 'awsaj (a thorny tree). Al-Hakim said: the 'awsaj was never subjected to anyone after him. Al-Kalbi said: it was of the myrtle (aas) of Paradise, ten cubits long, equal to Musa's height.

﴿Then behold, it was a serpent, plainly visible﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

The first: it was a male serpent (al-hayyah al-dhakar). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it was a yellow serpent with a mane around its neck (i'tamma al-hayyat al-sufr shi'ra' al-'unuq), related by al-Naqqash.

﴿Plainly visible﴾ has two interpretations:

The first: it was plainly visible as a serpent.

The second: it was plainly visible as a sign and a proof. Pharaoh had intended harm to Musa, but when the staff became a serpent gaping its mouth, he feared it and sought refuge with Musa, seeking protection, and his people fled in flight until some of them trampled on others. Ibn Zayd said: their gathering was at Alexandria. Al-Zajjaj said: it is related that the sorcerers numbered twelve thousand, and it was said: nineteen thousand.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"So what do you advise?"﴾ That is, what do you counsel, because it is not permissible for a follower to command the one he follows; so he made the counsel an command, since it is in its form.

His consulting them may bear two interpretations:

The first: he intended to win their sympathy because of his weakness of spirit.

The second: what he witnessed overwhelmed him, his intellect was bewildered, so he turned to their opinion, while he was saying "I am your Lord, the Most High," and the contradiction between the two matters was hidden from him through abandonment (khidhlan).(p-170)

The first: Delay him and his brother. This is what Ibn 'Abbas said.

As for their counsel to Pharaoh to postpone (dealing with) Moses and their prohibition to him of killing him, there are three aspects:

The third: God turned them away from that in order to make His religion firm and to support His Messenger.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-Uyun*) on Surah 26, verses 52–59**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, these are but a small band (shirdhimah qalilun)﴾. Regarding *al-shirdhimah* (a small group, remnant) there are two interpretations:

The first: they are the lowest of people and their most base, as said by al-Dahhak, and from it is the saying of al-A'sha:

؎ They are the slaves among their own tribes, for slaves, and you see them as a *shirdhimah*.

(p-171) The second: they are the remaining group of a great company, and the *shirdhimah* of anything is its small remainder.

It is said that the pieces cut from the excess of sandals' leather are *shararidh*, and for a shirt when it has worn out are *shararidh*. Abu 'Ubaydah recited:

؎ Winter has come and my shirt is worn-out rags, *shararidh*, at which the one who longs (for warmth) laughs.

There was disagreement about the number of the Children of Israel when Pharaoh said of them: "Indeed, they are a small band." There are four opinions:

The first: six hundred and ninety thousand. Muqatil said: one does not count the one under twenty for his youth, nor the one over sixty for his age. This is also the view of al-Suddi.

The third: they were six hundred thousand fighting men, as said by Qatadah.

The fourth: they were five hundred thousand and three thousand and five hundred. This number was considered small for two reasons:

The first: because of the great number of those who had been killed among them.

The second: because of the great number of those who were with him (Pharaoh). Al-Suddi related that at the head of his vanguard was Haman, with one thousand thousand and seven hundred thousand horses, among which there were no female horses. Al-Dahhak said they were seven thousand thousand.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed we are all wary (ḥādhirūn)﴾. This is the recitation of Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Abu 'Amr. The rest read ﴿ḥādhirūn﴾ (with the *dhal* dotted). In it there are four interpretations:

The first: that both are two dialects with one meaning. This was related by Ibn Shajarah and said by Abu 'Ubaydah, who cited the poet's verse:

؎ I was wary of death on his account alone, so nothing remains for me on his account to be wary of.

(p-172) The second: that *ḥadhir* is one who is naturally disposed to caution, and *ḥādhir* is one who actively takes caution. This was related by Ibn 'Isa.

The third: that *ḥadhir* is one who fears, and *ḥādhir* is one who prepares.

The fourth: that *ḥadhir* is one who is alert, and *ḥādhir* is one who takes up weapons, because weapons are called *ḥadhar*, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And take your precaution﴾ [al-Nisa': 102], meaning your weapons. Ibn 'Amir read:

*ḥādirūn* (with an undotted *dal*). Regarding its interpretation there are two views:

The first: strong, from their saying *jamal ḥādir*, when a camel is thick-bodied.

The second: hastening.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And treasures (kunūz)﴾. Regarding it there are three interpretations:

The first: storehouses.

The second: hidden stores.

The third: rivers, as said by al-Dahhak.

﴿And a noble station (maqām karīm)﴾. Regarding it there are three opinions:

The first: that they are pulpits, as said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid.

The second: the assemblies of rulers, related by Ibn 'Isa.

The third: fine dwellings, as said by Ibn Jubayr.

And it may admit a fourth: that they are the stables of horses, because leaders alone are tied up with them for number and adornment, so their station became the most honourable dwelling place.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 26, verses 60–77:

(p-173) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So they followed them at sunrise﴾. On this there are three opinions:

First: when the sun rose with its rays. This is the view of al-Suddi.

Second: when the earth became bright with light. This is the view of Qatadah.

Third: that is, toward the direction of the east (mashriq). This is the view of Abu 'Ubaydah.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is said "sharaqat al-shams" when the sun rises, and "ashraqat" when it shines.

It has been differed over regarding the delay of Pharaoh and his people behind Musa and the Children of Israel until they reached sunrise, on two views:

One: because they were occupied with burying their firstborn, for the plague had fallen upon them that night.

The second: because a cloud overshadowed them, so they feared and remained until morning, and then it dispersed from them.

It was also read as ﴿mushriqin﴾ with the doubled letter, meaning "toward the east," derived from their saying "sharraqa and gharraba," when one travels toward the east and the west.

﴿He said: "Never! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me."﴾ On this there are two meanings:

First: that is, He will guide me to the way.

Second: its meaning is, He will suffice me, this is the view of al-Suddi.

"Kalla" is a word used for restraint and deterrence. It is related that when Musa departed with the Children of Israel from Egypt, the moon grew dark upon them, so he said to his people: "What is this?" Their scholars said: "When Yusuf was at the point of death, he took a covenant upon us from Allah that we would not leave Egypt until we carry his bones with us." Musa said: "Then which of you knows where his grave is?" They said: "None knows it except an old woman of the Children of Israel." So he sent for her (p-174) and said: "Show me the grave of Yusuf." She said: "No, by Allah, I will not do so until you give me my due right." He said: "And what is your due right?" She said: "My due right is that I be with you in Paradise." It weighed heavily upon him, and it was said to him: "Give her her due right." So she showed them the place, and they dug it up and extracted his bones. When they lifted them, the path was like the light of day.

Abu Burdah related from Abu Musa: "The Prophet ﷺ stayed with a Bedouin, and he honoured him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'What is your need?' He said: 'A she-camel that I may saddle, and goats that I may milk.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Are you unable to be like the old woman of the Children of Israel?' The Companions said: 'And what is the old woman of the Children of Israel?' So he related to them the condition of this old woman who judged upon Musa that she would be with him in Paradise."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then We revealed to Musa: "Strike the sea with your staff," and it parted﴾. Ikrimah related from Ibn 'Abbas that when Musa reached the sea and Pharaoh pursued him, his young servant Yusha' ibn Nun said to him: "Where has your Lord commanded you?" He said: "Ahead of you," pointing to the sea. Then he mentioned that he was commanded to strike the sea with his staff, so he struck it, and it split for him into twelve paths, for they were twelve tribes, and each tribe had a path; the width of each path was two farsakh.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the sea had been still and not moving, but when it was the night Musa struck it with the staff, it began to swell and recede.

Al-Naqqash related that Musa struck the sea with his staff when four hours of the day had passed, and it was Monday, the tenth of Muharram, which is the day of 'Ashura'. He said: the sea was the Nile, between Aylah and Egypt, and they crossed it in two hours, so it became six hours.

﴿So every part was like a mighty mountain﴾, that is, like a great mountain. Imru' al-Qays said:

*"While a man was among the living, a mountain, the people threw him from nearby, and he leaned over."*

The tribes did not see one another, so each tribe said: "Our companions have perished." Musa called upon his Lord, and He made in each partition something like windows until they saw one another.

(p-175) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We brought the others near there﴾. On this there are two meanings:

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 26, verse 78–82:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Who created me, and it is He who guides me﴾, has two interpretations:

One: Who created me with His blessing, and it is He who guides me to His obedience.

The second: Who created me for His obedience, and it is He who guides me to His Paradise. If it is said: this is an attribute of all creation, so how did Ibrahim make it evidence of his own guidance, when no one else was guided by it?

It is said: He mentioned it as an argument for the obligation of obedience, because whoever bestows a favour must be obeyed and not disobeyed, so that others are bound to the obedience to which he himself is bound. This is a sound argument (ilzam). Then he elaborated this by enumerating His blessings upon him and upon them, saying: ﴿And who feeds me and gives me drink﴾ ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾. This was an argument against them, since they agreed with him on it. Then he said: ﴿And who causes me to die, then gives me life﴾. He said this as a proof (istidlal), not as an argument (ihtijaj), because they disagreed with him on it. So he showed them that what they agreed with him upon necessitates what they disagreed with him upon.

Some of those who go deep into subtle meanings (al-muta'ammiqah fi ghawamid al-ma'ani) permitted a figurative reading, departing thereby from its apparent meaning to what the immediate judgment of reason rejects. So he interpreted ﴿And who feeds me and gives me drink﴾ as: He feeds me the sweetness of faith and gives me the sweetness of acceptance.

Regarding His saying: ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾, there are two interpretations:

One: When I fall ill through disobedience to Him, He cures me with His mercy.

The second: When I fall ill from enduring the people, He cures me by witnessing the Truth.

They interpreted His saying: ﴿And who causes me to die, then gives me life﴾ in three ways:

The first: who causes me to die through sins and gives me life through acts of obedience.

The second: He causes me to die through fear and gives me life through hope.

The third: He causes me to die through greed and gives me life through contentment.

These are interpretations that move beyond the category of probability into the realm of mere curiosity; therefore we have mentioned them, although omitting them from our book would be better.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Who created me, and it is He who guides me﴾, has two interpretations:

One: Who created me with His blessing, and it is He who guides me to His obedience.

The second: Who created me for His obedience, and it is He who guides me to His Paradise. If it is said: this is an attribute of all creation, so how did Ibrahim make it evidence of his own guidance, when no one else was guided by it?

It is said: He mentioned it as an argument for the obligation of obedience, because whoever bestows a favour must be obeyed and not disobeyed, so that others are bound to the obedience to which he himself is bound. This is a sound argument (ilzam). Then he elaborated this by enumerating His blessings upon him and upon them, saying: ﴿And who feeds me and gives me drink﴾ ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾. This was an argument against them, since they agreed with him on it. Then he said: ﴿And who causes me to die, then gives me life﴾. He said this as a proof (istidlal), not as an argument (ihtijaj), because they disagreed with him on it. So he showed them that what they agreed with him upon necessitates what they disagreed with him upon.

Some of those who go deep into subtle meanings (al-muta'ammiqah fi ghawamid al-ma'ani) permitted a figurative reading, departing thereby from its apparent meaning to what the immediate judgment of reason rejects. So he interpreted ﴿And who feeds me and gives me drink﴾ as: He feeds me the sweetness of faith and gives me the sweetness of acceptance.

Regarding His saying: ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾, there are two interpretations:

One: When I fall ill through disobedience to Him, He cures me with His mercy.

The second: When I fall ill from enduring the people, He cures me by witnessing the Truth.

They interpreted His saying: ﴿And who causes me to die, then gives me life﴾ in three ways:

The first: who causes me to die through sins and gives me life through acts of obedience.

The second: He causes me to die through fear and gives me life through hope.

The third: He causes me to die through greed and gives me life through contentment.

These are interpretations that move beyond the category of probability into the realm of mere curiosity; therefore we have mentioned them, although omitting them from our book would be better.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 26, verses 83–89:

Allah's words: ﴿My Lord, grant me wisdom (ḥukm)﴾. On this there are four interpretations:

First: it is intellect (lubb). This was said by ʿIkrimah.

Second: it is knowledge (ʿilm). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Third: it is the Qur'an. This was said by Mujahid.

Fourth: it is prophethood (nubuwwah). This was said by al-Suddi.

It may also admit a fifth: that it is reaching the truth in judgment.

﴿And join me with the righteous﴾. ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: with the prophets and the believers.

It may admit two meanings:

One: among Your chosen servants in this world.

The second: with the reward of the righteous in the Hereafter and their neighborhood in Paradise.

(p-177) Allah's words: ﴿And make for me a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations﴾. On this there are three sayings:

First: a good reputation among all nations. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah, and it is called a "tongue" because it is conveyed by the tongue.

Second: that people of every religious community believe in him. This was said by Layth ibn Abi Sulaym.

Third: that He make among his descendants one who speaks the truth after him. This was said by ʿAli ibn ʿIsa.

It may admit a fourth: that he be one who confirms all the religious communities, and he was granted this.

Allah's words: ﴿And forgive my father﴾, to the end of the verse.

Regarding his father there are two sayings:

First: that he concealed faith and displayed disbelief. In this case, seeking forgiveness for him is valid.

Second, and it is the more apparent: that he was an unbeliever outwardly and inwardly.

On this basis, regarding his seeking forgiveness for him there are two sayings:

First: that he asked that He forgive him in this world and not punish him in it.

Second: that he asked that He forgive him the sins upon him which would be removed by His pardon.

Allah's words: ﴿with a sound heart (qalb)﴾. On this there are five aspects:

First: free from doubt. This was said by Mujahid.

Second: free from polytheism. This was said by al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd.

Third: free from sins, since when the heart is sound, the limbs are sound.

Fourth: that it is sincere. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Fifth: that it is one who advises His creation. This was said by ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Hatim.

It may admit a sixth: sound of heart from fear on the Day of Resurrection, due to the good tidings previously mentioned at the time of witnessing.(p-178)

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 26, verses 90–104:**

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So they will be thrown into it, they and the deviators﴾. Regarding "fa-kubkibu" there are four interpretations:

First: its meaning is that they are gathered into it, that is, into the Fire. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: they are cast into it on their faces. This was said by Ibn Zayd and Qutrub.

Third: they are turned upside down into it, on their heads. This was said by al-Suddi and Ibn Qutaybah.

Fourth: some of them are overturned upon others. This was said by al-Yazidi, and the poet said:

؎ The Messenger of Allah says to them, when we have hurled them, like heaps, into the pit

﴿They and the deviators﴾ means the gods that they worshipped.

Regarding "al-Ghawun" (the deviators) there are two views:

First: the polytheists. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: the devils. This was said by Qatadah.

﴿And the hosts of Iblis, all of them﴾. Regarding them there are two views:

First: they are his helpers from among the jinn.

Second: his followers from among mankind.

Second: the near relative by lineage. It is said "hamma al-shayʾ" when a thing has drawn near, and from it comes "al-hummah" (fever), because it brings near the term (of life). Qays ibn Dhurayh said:

؎ Perhaps today Lubna's meeting has drawn near, and among some trials, what has drawn near is certainly befalling.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 26, verses 90–104:**

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So they will be thrown into it, they and the deviators﴾. Regarding "fa-kubkibu" there are four interpretations:

First: its meaning is that they are gathered into it, that is, into the Fire. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: they are cast into it on their faces. This was said by Ibn Zayd and Qutrub.

Third: they are turned upside down into it, on their heads. This was said by al-Suddi and Ibn Qutaybah.

Fourth: some of them are overturned upon others. This was said by al-Yazidi, and the poet said:

؎ The Messenger of Allah says to them, when we have hurled them, like heaps, into the pit

﴿They and the deviators﴾ means the gods that they worshipped.

Regarding "al-Ghawun" (the deviators) there are two views:

First: the polytheists. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: the devils. This was said by Qatadah.

﴿And the hosts of Iblis, all of them﴾. Regarding them there are two views:

First: they are his helpers from among the jinn.

Second: his followers from among mankind.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So we have no intercessors﴾. Regarding them there are two views:

First: the angels.

Second: from among the people.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 26, verse 105–115:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the lowest-born have followed you﴾. Concerning it there are five opinions:

First: they are those who ask (people for things) and are not content.

Second: they are the arrogant.

Third: they are the lowest and basest of people. This is the view of Qatadah.

Fourth: they are the weavers. This is the view of Mujahid.

Fifth: they are the cobblers (al-asakifah). This is the view of Ibn Bahr.

And it may be a sixth: they are the people of all the base professions.

"His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You will surely be among those stoned﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions:

First: by stoning with rocks. This was said by Qatadah.

Second: by killing. This was said by Muhammad ibn al-Hasan.

Third: by reviling. This was said by al-Suddi.

Abu Dawud said:

"They [the wayward ones of Ma'add] turned me away from addressing them, just as they turn away from the men of intellect, like bowls [of food]."

(p-180) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So decide between me and them with a decision﴾. Qatadah and al-Suddi said: "Be with us, and judge between me and them with a judgment, which is that You save him and those who are with him of the believers and separate the disbelievers." Nuh did not invoke his Lord against them except after He had informed him, ﴿that none of your people will believe except those who have already believed﴾ [Hud: 36], and then he prayed against them.

**Its meaning, in the words of His saying ﴿Do you build on every high place a monument, playing?﴾, has six interpretations:**

**First:** *al-Rayʿ* (ريع) is the road. This was said by al-Suddi, and from it is the verse of al-Musayyab ibn ʿAli:

*In the mirage that lifts it and lowers it, a road (rayʿ) gleams as though it were a white cloth.*

*Al-Sahl* (السحل) is a white garment; he likened the road to it.

**Second:** It is a small pass (al-thaniyya al-saghira). This was said by Mujahid.

**Third:** It is the market. Al-Kalbi related this.

**Fourth:** It is the wide passage between two mountains. This was said by Mujahid.

**Fifth:** It is the mountains. This was said by Abu Sakhr.

**Sixth:** It is the elevated place of the land. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. Dhu al-Rummah said:

*Its primary feathers are dappled, shining above its high ground (rayʿihi), the dew of its night glistening in its plumage.*

(p-181) **﴿A sign, you play﴾**: in the word *āya* (آية) there are three aspects:

**First:** It is the buildings. This was said by Mujahid.

**Second:** It is the landmarks. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

**Third:** It is the dovecotes. Ibn Abi Najih related this.

Regarding *al-ʿabath* (العبث), the play, there are two views:

**First:** It is amusement and play. This was said by ʿAtiyya.

**Second:** It is the plundering of the tax collectors (al-ʿashshārūn) of the wealth of those who pass by them. This was said by al-Kalbi.

**﴿And you take palaces, that perhaps you may live forever﴾**: concerning *maṣāniʿ* (مصانع) there are three sayings:

**First:** They are lofty palaces. This was said by Mujahid, and from it is the verse of the poet:

*We left their homes desolate, and we demolished the palaces (al-maṣāniʿ) and the towers (al-burūj).*

**Second:** They are reservoirs of water beneath the earth. This was said by Qatada, and from it is the verse of Labid:

*We wore out, but the lasting stars do not wear out, and the mountains and the reservoirs (al-maṣāniʿ) remain after us.*

**Third:** They are dovecotes. This was said by al-Suddi.

**﴿That perhaps you may live forever﴾** means: as though you will live forever by building these dwellings. Qatada related that in some recitations it reads: *"as though you are abiding (khālidūn)."*

**﴿And when you strike, you strike like tyrants﴾**: concerning this there are three aspects:

**First:** They are strong. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

**Second:** It is striking with whips. This was said by Mujahid.

**Third:** It is killing with the sword without right. Yahya ibn Salam related this.

Al-Kalbi said: It is killing in anger.

It may also bear a fourth meaning: that it is taking to account for intentional and unintentional acts without pardon or leniency.

**Third:** It is killing with the sword without right. Yahya ibn Salam related this.

Al-Kalbi said: It is killing in anger.

It may also bear a fourth meaning: that it is taking to account for intentional and unintentional acts without pardon or leniency.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿This is nothing but the habit of the former peoples﴾ (khuluq al-awwalin). There are four interpretations of it:

First: it is the religion (din) of the former peoples. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: it is like the way (ka-daʾb) of the former peoples. This was said by Mujahid.

Third: it is the custom (ʿadah) of the former peoples. This was said by al-Farra'.

Fourth: it means that the former peoples before us used to die and were not resurrected nor called to account. This was said by Qatadah.

God's statement, Exalted is He: ﴿And palm trees with delicate spathes﴾ has ten interpretations (ta'wilat, meanings):

First: It is the moist and soft (dates), said by ʿIkrima.

Second: It is the dates that are slightly blemished (al-mudhannab), said by Ibn Jubayr.

Third: It is the one that has no pit (nawa), said by al-Hasan.

Fourth: It is the one that is crushed and crumbles when touched, said by Mujahid.

Fifth: It is the one whose parts are tightly pressed against each other, said by Abu Sakhr.

Sixth: It is the spathe (tal') when it splits open and turns green, said by al-Dahhak.

Seventh: It is the ripe and mature, said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Eighth: It is the one that is compact before its skin splits open, related by Ibn Shajara. The poet said:

"As if a load being unveiled upon it, delicate, with no cracks perceptible in it."

Ninth: It is the soft and loose, said by al-Hasan.

Tenth: It is the fine and subtle, said by al-Kalbi.

It is possible that al-hadim (delicate) means the one that aids digestion (al-hadim al-mari'), that is, easy to digest.

Al-tal' (spathe) is a noun derived from al-tuluʿ (emergence), which means appearance. From it come the rising of the sun, the moon and plants.

God's statement, Exalted is He: (fārihīn, "exultant"). Abu ʿAmr, Ibn Kathir and Nafiʿ recited it as فَرِهِينَ (fariheen, without alif). The rest recited it as ﴿فارِهِينَ﴾ (fārihīn, with alif). As for the one who recites فَرِهِينَ (fariheen), there are six interpretations:

First: it means greedy (sharihin), said by Mujahid.

Second: it means admiring or self-impressed (muʿjabin), said by Khuṣayf.

Third: it means secure (amin), said by Qatada.

Fourth: it means joyful (fariḥin), related by Ibn Shajara.

Fifth: it means insolent and arrogant (bataran ashirin), said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Sixth: it means choosing or selective (mutakhayyirin), said by al-Kalbi.

From this is the poet's saying:

"To a proud man who vies with every matter I have aimed at him, to test his character."

As for the one who recites ﴿فارِهِينَ﴾ (fārihīn), there are four interpretations:

First: its meaning is clever (kayyisin), said by al-…

Second: skilful (ḥādhiqin), said by Abu Salih, derived from the excellence (farahah) of craftsmanship; this is also the view of Ibn ʿAbbas.

Third: capable (qadirin), said by Ibn Bahr.

Fourth: it is the plural of fārih, and al-fārih means exuberant (al-marah), said by Abu ʿUbayda, who cited the verse of ʿAdi ibn al-Raqqaʿ al-Ghanawi:

"I do not yield when a hardship grips, and you will never see me in good state, with a fārih al-labab (a strong, proud chest-strap)."

That is, from the labab (the breast-strap of a saddle).

First: it means greedy (sharihin), said by Mujahid.

Second: it means admiring or self-impressed (muʿjabin), said by Khuṣayf.

Third: it means secure (amin), said by Qatada.

Fourth: it means joyful (fariḥin), related by Ibn Shajara.

Fifth: it means insolent and arrogant (bataran ashirin), said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Sixth: it means choosing or selective (mutakhayyirin), said by al-Kalbi.

From this is the poet's saying:

"To a proud man who vies with every matter I have aimed at him, to test his character."

As for the one who recites ﴿فارِهِينَ﴾ (fārihīn), there are four interpretations:

First: its meaning is clever (kayyisin), said by al-…

Second: skilful (ḥādhiqin), said by Abu Salih, derived from the excellence (farahah) of craftsmanship; this is also the view of Ibn ʿAbbas.

Third: capable (qadirin), said by Ibn Bahr.

Fourth: it is the plural of fārih, and al-fārih means exuberant (al-marah), said by Abu ʿUbayda, who cited the verse of ʿAdi ibn al-Raqqaʿ al-Ghanawi:

"I do not yield when a hardship grips, and you will never see me in good state, with a fārih al-labab (a strong, proud chest-strap)."

That is, from the labab (the breast-strap of a saddle).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You are only one of those who are bewitched﴾ has seven interpretations (ta'wilat):

First: "from those who are bewitched (al-masḥurīn)." This was said by Mujahid.

Second: "from those who are intoxicated (al-sakrānīn)." This was said by Qatada.

Third: "from among the created beings (al-makhlūqīn)." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Fourth: "from those who are deceived (al-makhdū'īn)." This was said by Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah.

Fifth: that the musaḥḥar is one who has nothing and owns nothing, that is, one who is poor (al-muqill). The meaning is: you are not a king who would remain. This is the meaning of the saying of al-Kalbi.

Sixth: "one who has siḥr," that is, a charm (ruqya). This was related by Ibn 'Isa.

Seventh: "one who eats and drinks." This was related by Ibn Shajara, and from it is the saying of Labid:

"If you ask us what we are about, we are but sparrows among this sustained (musaḥḥar) race of humankind."

That is, one who is kept alive (mu'allal) by food and drink. Imru' al-Qays said:

"We find ourselves intent upon a matter of the unseen, and we are sustained (nus'har) by food and drink."

(p-185)

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 26, verses 159–184:**

Allah's words: ﴿And weigh with the upright balance﴾. Concerning it there are five interpretations:

First: it is the *qabban* (a steelyard balance), said by al-Hasan.

Second: it is iron, narrated by Ibn al-Mubarak.

Third: it is the *mi'yar* (standard measure), said by al-Dahhak.

Fourth: it is the *mizan* (scale), said by al-Akhfash and al-Kalbi.

Fifth: it is justice.

Those who hold this interpretation differ over whether the word is Arabic or Roman (Greek). Mujahid and al-Sha'bi said: it is justice in Roman. Abu Ubayda and Ibn Shajara said: it is Arabic, and its root is *al-qist*, which means justice. From this is Allah's words: ﴿standing firm in justice﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18], meaning, with justice.

Allah's words: ﴿And do not commit abuse on the earth, spreading corruption﴾. Concerning it there are two views:

First: its meaning is, do not walk in it in acts of disobedience, said by Abu Malik.

Second: do not walk in it with injustice after it has been set right by justice, said by Ibn al-Musayyib.

It may also bear a third meaning: the mischief of the corrupter is that which harms others and does not benefit himself.

Allah's words: ﴿and the *jibilla*﴾ means the creation. Imru' al-Qays said:

*Death is the greatest of events that pass over the creation.*

﴿the earlier ones﴾ means the past nations. The Arabs pronounce the *jim* and *ba'* of *al-jibilla* with a kasra, and they may also pronounce them with a damma, and sometimes they drop the *ha'* (of *jibillah*), as Allah said: ﴿And he had certainly led astray from among you a great multitude﴾ [Ya-Sin: 62], where the word is *jibillan*. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

*Fates that bring near the deaths to their people openly, and enjoy the familiar company of the creation.*

(p-186)

Third: a punishment. This is what al-Suddī said. The poet said:

؎ My love for her is sincere and gathered in the heart, and her love, know it, is a punishment for what is above (me)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 26, verses 192–195:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It was brought down by the Trustworthy Spirit﴾. He means the Qur'an.

﴿The Trustworthy Spirit﴾: he means Jibril (Gabriel).

﴿Upon your heart﴾: he means Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿That you may be among the warners﴾: he means for your community.

﴿In a clear Arabic tongue﴾: he means that the language of the Qur'an is clear Arabic, because the one upon whom it was sent down is an Arab, those addressed by it are Arabs, and because it challenged the eloquent of the Arabs with its eloquence.

Regarding the Arabic tongue there are two opinions:

The first: it is the tongue of Jurhum, as said by Abu Barzah.

The second: it is the tongue of Quraysh, as said by Mujahid.

Allah's statement: ﴿And indeed, it is in the scriptures of the former peoples﴾, meaning the books of the former peoples, from the Torah and the Gospel and other books.

On this verse there are three interpretations:

First: that what is meant is the mention of the Qur'an in the scriptures of the former peoples. This is the view of Qatadah.

Second: the sending of Muhammad (ﷺ) in the scriptures of the former peoples. This is the view of al-Suddi.

Third: the mention of your religion and the description of your community in the scriptures of the former peoples. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 26, verses 200–209:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Thus We have caused it to enter﴾ (kadhalika salaknahu). There are three opinions concerning it:

First: "Thus We caused shirk (associating partners with God) to enter [the hearts of the criminals]." This was said by Anas ibn Malik.

Second: It means denial (al-takdhib). This was said by Yahya ibn Sallam.

Third: It means hardness of heart (al-qaswa). This was said by Ikrimah.

The Word of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Who sees you when you stand﴾ has four interpretations:

First: when you stand in prayer. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās.

Second: when you rise from your bedding and your sitting place. This is the view of al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

(p-189) Third: meaning that He sees you standing, sitting, and in all your states. This is the view of Qatādah.

Fourth: meaning when you are alone. This is the view of al-Ḥasan, and "standing" is then an expression for being alone, since one reaches solitude by rising from its opposite.

The Word of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿and your movement among those who prostrate﴾ has six interpretations:

First: from one prophet to another, until He brought you forth as a prophet. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās.

Second: He sees your movements in your prayer, in your bowing and your prostration. This is related by Ibn Jarīr.

Third: that you see your movements in prayer from behind you as you see with your eyes what is in front of you. This is the view of Mujāhid.

Fourth: its meaning is "and your conduct among the people," because of his turning in their affairs and their actions. This is the view of al-Ḥasan.

Fifth: the turning of your remembrance and your attributes on the tongues of the prophets before you.

Sixth: that the meaning of His Word ﴿Who sees you when you stand﴾ is when you pray alone, and ﴿and your movement among those who prostrate﴾ is when you pray in congregation. This is the view of Qatādah.

A seventh possibility is also admitted: ﴿Who sees you when you stand﴾ for the struggle against the polytheists, and ﴿and your movement among those who prostrate﴾ in what you intend concerning the Muslims and what you legislate of the rulings of the religion.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 26, verses 221–227:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the poets—the deviators follow them﴾, meaning: when they become angry, they revile. Concerning them there are four opinions:

The first: they are the devils. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: they are the polytheists. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: they are the foolish. This was said by al-Dahhak.

(p-190) The fourth: they are the transmitters (al-ruwat). This was said by Ibn Abbas.

﴿Do you not see that they wander in every valley?﴾ Concerning this there are three aspects:

The first: they take up every kind of speech. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: they plunge into every idle talk. This was said by Qutrub, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Indeed I apologize to you for what I did, when I was wandering in error."

The third: it is that they praise a people with falsehood and blame a people with falsehood. This was said by Qatadah.

Concerning "al-HA'im" (the one who wanders) there are two aspects:

The first: that it is the one who opposes in intention. This was said by Abu Ubayda.

The second: that it is the one who exceeds the limit.

﴿And that they say what they do not do﴾, meaning: what they mention in their poetry of falsehood, by way of praise, blame, comparison, or amorous lament.

﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. Its implied meaning: then they are not followed by the deviators, and they do not say what they do not do.

It is narrated that Abdullah ibn Rawahah, Ka'b ibn Malik and Hassan ibn Thabit came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when there was revealed ﴿And the poets—the deviators follow them﴾, and they wept before him and said: "We are ruined, O Messenger of Allah," (p-191) so Allah revealed ﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. He recited it to them until he reached His saying: ﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾, and he said: "You are they."

﴿And they remember Allah much﴾. Concerning this there are two aspects:

The first: in their poetry.

The second: in their speech.

﴿And they defend themselves after they have been wronged﴾, meaning: they responded to the polytheists with what the polytheists used to satirize the believers with, and they fought them over it, in support of the believers and as retribution against the polytheists.

﴿And those who have wronged will know what return they will be returned to﴾. This is a warning directed at whoever among the poets satirized the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and at every disbeliever, poet or not: they will know on the Day of Resurrection what destination they will arrive at and what place of return they will return to, because their destination is the Fire, which is the worst destination, and their return is to punishment, which is the worst return.

The difference between "al-munqalab" (the return) and "al-marji'" (the place of return) is that al-munqalab is the transition to the opposite of what one is in, while al-marji' is the returning from a state one is in to a state one was previously upon. Thus the one who arrives at a place of return has undergone a transition, but not every transition is a return.

﴿Do you not see that they wander in every valley?﴾ Concerning this there are three aspects:

The first: they take up every kind of speech. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: they plunge into every idle talk. This was said by Qutrub, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Indeed I apologize to you for what I did, when I was wandering in error."

The third: it is that they praise a people with falsehood and blame a people with falsehood. This was said by Qatadah.

Concerning "al-HA'im" (the one who wanders) there are two aspects:

The first: that it is the one who opposes in intention. This was said by Abu Ubayda.

The second: that it is the one who exceeds the limit.

﴿And that they say what they do not do﴾, meaning: what they mention in their poetry of falsehood, by way of praise, blame, comparison, or amorous lament.

﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. Its implied meaning: then they are not followed by the deviators, and they do not say what they do not do.

It is narrated that Abdullah ibn Rawahah, Ka'b ibn Malik and Hassan ibn Thabit came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when there was revealed ﴿And the poets—the deviators follow them﴾, and they wept before him and said: "We are ruined, O Messenger of Allah," (p-191) so Allah revealed ﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. He recited it to them until he reached His saying: ﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾, and he said: "You are they."

﴿And they remember Allah much﴾. Concerning this there are two aspects:

The first: in their poetry.

The second: in their speech.

﴿And they defend themselves after they have been wronged﴾, meaning: they responded to the polytheists with what the polytheists used to satirize the believers with, and they fought them over it, in support of the believers and as retribution against the polytheists.

﴿And those who have wronged will know what return they will be returned to﴾. This is a warning directed at whoever among the poets satirized the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and at every disbeliever, poet or not: they will know on the Day of Resurrection what destination they will arrive at and what place of return they will return to, because their destination is the Fire, which is the worst destination, and their return is to punishment, which is the worst return.

The difference between "al-munqalab" (the return) and "al-marji'" (the place of return) is that al-munqalab is the transition to the opposite of what one is in, while al-marji' is the returning from a state one is in to a state one was previously upon. Thus the one who arrives at a place of return has undergone a transition, but not every transition is a return.
